skills.presentation: Commonly occurs in seborrhea-rich areas such as the face, anterior chest, and back. Lesions are pleomorphic: comedones (whiteheads/blackheads), inflammatory papules, pustules, nodules, cysts, and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation or scars.

first_questions: Which areas are the acne lesions mainly distributed in (face, chest, back)? How long have they been present?
Are the lesions mainly comedones, small red bumps, and pustules with whiteheads, or are there deeper and larger indurated nodules/cysts?
Do you usually have excessive oiliness? Is there obvious pain or tenderness?
followup_questions: For female patients, are menstrual cycles regular? Do acne lesions clearly worsen before menstruation? (screen for hyperandrogenism/PCOS)
What are your usual dietary and sleep habits (do you prefer sweets, dairy products, fried foods, or staying up late)?
What topical or oral medications have you used previously? Do you have a habit of squeezing acne lesions yourself?
stop_conditions: Clinical acne grading (mild/moderate/severe) and main lesion morphology have been clarified
Endocrine-related clues such as polycystic ovary syndrome have been screened
Previous responses to skincare products and drug treatment are clearly understood

essential: Dermatology specialist visual inspection and Wood's lamp/dermoscopy (to assess lesion type, severity, and Malassezia fluorescence)
if_suspected: Sex hormone panel + gynecological ultrasound (women with hirsutism, hair loss, menstrual irregularity suspected of polycystic ovary syndrome)
Liver function, lipids, complete blood count (mandatory before planned oral isotretinoin)
Bacterial culture and antimicrobial susceptibility of secretions (severe recurrent pustules that do not heal)
avoid: Ordering broad autoimmune panels without indication for mild-to-moderate acne
Ordering head CT/MRI without cranial neurological symptoms

first_line: Topical drugs: retinoids (adapalene gel, all-trans retinoic acid cream) for comedones and anti-inflammatory effect + benzoyl peroxide (BPO) or topical antibiotics (clindamycin gel)
Moderate-to-severe acne: oral tetracycline antibiotics (doxycycline/minocycline) or oral isotretinoin capsules
Adjust to a low-GI diet and avoid squeezing.
safety_warnings: Isotretinoin is strongly teratogenic! Women of childbearing age must use strict contraception during treatment and for at least 3 months after discontinuation
Monitor liver function and lipids during treatment
Topical retinoids are photosensitizing and locally irritating; use at night with light avoidance and start at low concentration to build tolerance
Oral doxycycline/minocycline are contraindicated in children under 8 years and pregnant women; during treatment, use sun protection to prevent photosensitivity
personalization: Mild acne (mainly comedones): topical adapalene gel or benzoyl peroxide only
Moderate inflammatory papules and pustules: topical BPO + adapalene, oral doxycycline for 6-8 weeks
Severe nodulocystic type (grade III/IV): oral isotretinoin is first choice, reaching cumulative dose to prevent recurrence

skills.presentation: Sudden onset of wheals of varying size and irregular shape (edematous erythema and pale raised lesions) with intense itching; lesions wax and wane, and an individual wheal usually resolves spontaneously within 24 hours without leaving marks, while new lesions may appear at other sites after resolution; severe cases may be accompanied by angioedema, laryngeal edema, abdominal pain, diarrhea, or anaphylactic shock.

first_questions: How long have the red wheals (mosquito-bite-like bumps) on your body been present? How many hours does each bump usually take to resolve?
After resolution, does the skin leave marks or hyperpigmentation? How severe is the itching?
Before the outbreak, did you eat seafood, nuts, beef or mutton, or use antibiotics or other drugs, or come into contact with pollen or cold/heat stimuli?
followup_questions: During attacks, do you have breathing difficulty, throat tightness, hoarseness, or wheezing? (screen for laryngeal edema)
Do you have abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea? Do you have dizziness, visual blackout, or palpitations? (screen for shock)
Have the recurrent attacks lasted more than 6 weeks? (distinguish acute from chronic urticaria)
stop_conditions: Acute/chronic course and the typical migratory wheals resolving within 24 hours have been clarified
Critical signs such as laryngeal edema and anaphylactic shock have been strictly excluded
Possible allergens, physical triggers, and previous medication history have been clearly collected

essential: Dermatology specialist physical examination (dermatographism test)
Complete blood count (eosinophil count, total white blood cell count)
if_suspected: Serum total IgE and specific allergen IgE testing (sIgE)
C-reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) (to screen for infectious triggers)
Thyroid function and thyroid autoantibodies (for chronic refractory urticaria, to screen for autoimmune thyroiditis)
Helicobacter pylori breath test (for chronic urticaria, to screen for chronic gastrointestinal infection)
avoid: Blind skin tissue biopsy during acute attacks when no purpura-like lesions remain after wheals
Abuse of whole-body CT scans without clear evidence of poisoning

first_line: First choice: second-generation non-sedating antihistamines (e.g., loratadine, cetirizine, levocetirizine, ebastine, desloratadine)
Topical calamine lotion to relieve itching
Acute severe cases with laryngeal edema or shock: immediately intramuscular epinephrine (1:1000, 0.3-0.5 ml) and give oxygen, intravenous glucocorticoids.
safety_warnings: Patients with breathing difficulty, laryngeal edema, or decreased blood pressure have a fatal emergency; do not give only oral antihistamines—immediate resuscitation and intramuscular epinephrine are required
First-generation antihistamines (e.g., chlorpheniramine, diphenhydramine) have central sedative effects and are contraindicated for workers at heights, drivers, and machine operators
Avoid long-term dependence on systemic glucocorticoids for chronic urticaria
personalization: Chronic urticaria inadequately controlled with standard-dose second-generation antihistamines: increase the dose to 2-4 times, or combine with another class of second-generation antihistamines
Refractory chronic spontaneous urticaria: consider biologic omalizumab or cyclosporine
Pediatric urticaria: use antihistamine drops/syrups suitable for children (e.g., cetirizine drops)

skills.presentation: Typical psoriasis vulgaris presents as red papules or plaques with well-defined borders and multiple layers of dry silvery-white scales on the surface; gently scraping off the scales reveals a film phenomenon, and further scraping off the film reveals pinpoint bleeding (Auspitz sign). It is often accompanied by itching of varying severity and commonly occurs on the scalp, extensor aspects of the limbs (elbows and knees), and back.

first_questions: How long have the red plaques on your body been present? Is there easily shed silvery-white scaling on the surface?
Which areas are the plaques mainly distributed on (scalp, elbows, knees, back)?
Do you have thickened nails, pitted depressions (nail pitting), or swelling and pain in the joints of the hands and feet?
followup_questions: After scratching or scraping off the scales, is there a thin film underneath and pinpoint bleeding red spots?
Is there anyone in your family with similar skin disease?
Recently, have you had a cold or sore throat (streptococcal infection), taken certain medications, or been under high mental stress?
stop_conditions: The triad of erythema, silvery-white scales, film phenomenon, and pinpoint bleeding has been confirmed
Clinical subtype has been identified (vulgaris, psoriatic arthritis, pustular, erythrodermic)
Triggering/aggravating factors and joint involvement have been clearly collected

essential: Dermatology specialist visual inspection and dermoscopy (uniformly distributed loop-hair-like/dotted vessels on a red background and white scales)
if_suspected: Skin histopathological biopsy (parakeratosis with Munro microabscesses, acanthosis, elongated and edematous dermal papillae; used to confirm atypical difficult lesions)
Joint X-ray/MRI (for joint redness, swelling, and pain suggesting psoriatic arthritis)
Antistreptolysin O (ASO) and throat swab culture (for guttate psoriasis, to screen for streptococcal infection)
avoid: Systemic abuse of oral glucocorticoids for psoriasis vulgaris (after discontinuation, it can easily induce rebound of fatal erythrodermic or generalized pustular psoriasis)
Ordering broad tumor marker screening without indication

first_line: Topical drugs: glucocorticoids (e.g., halometasone, mometasone furoate) combined with vitamin D3 derivatives (calcipotriol ointment), or fixed-combination products (calcipotriol betamethasone ointment)
Emollient basic care
Moderate-to-severe patients: narrowband ultraviolet B (NB-UVB) phototherapy
Systemic therapy (methotrexate, acitretin, cyclosporine) or targeted biologics (e.g., secukinumab, ustekinumab, adalimumab).
safety_warnings: Oral or intravenous systemic glucocorticoids are absolutely prohibited for psoriasis vulgaris to prevent severe rebound that may be life-threatening
Acitretin is strongly teratogenic; women of childbearing age must use strict contraception during treatment and for 2 years after discontinuation
Monitor liver and kidney function and bone marrow hematopoiesis during oral methotrexate
Before using biologics, strictly screen for active tuberculosis, hepatitis B, and severe active infection
personalization: Mild plaque type (BSA <3%): topical calcipotriol ointment + weak-to-medium potency steroid + moisturizing emollient only
Guttate psoriasis (mostly seen in adolescents and children after pharyngitis): combine oral penicillins for anti-infection and anti-inflammatory treatment and phototherapy
Psoriatic arthritis: prioritize TNF-α inhibitors or IL-17A inhibitors and other biologics to prevent bone and joint destruction early

skills.presentation: Clustered vesicles at mucocutaneous junctions (angles of the mouth, lip margins, around the nostrils, or external genitalia) on an erythematous base; after rupture, the vesicles erode and form crusts, accompanied by local burning, stinging, or mild itching; the course is 1-2 weeks, and recurrences easily occur at the same or nearby sites during fever, cold exposure, fatigue, or immunocompromise.

first_questions: Are the vesicles located around the lips, around the nose, or on the external genitalia? How many days have they been present?
Before the vesicles appeared, was there local heat, tingling, or burning pain?
Have these vesicles recurred repeatedly at the same site before?
followup_questions: Recently, have you had a cold, fever, stayed up late, sun exposure, or extreme fatigue?
Have the vesicles ruptured and oozed yellow fluid and formed crusts? Is there severe neuralgia or spread to other parts of the body?
Do you have a history of external genital contact, or does your sexual partner have similar lesions? (screen for genital herpes HSV-2)
stop_conditions: The distribution of clustered vesicles, burning prodrome, and recurrent course have been clarified
Primary versus recurrent infection has been distinguished
Herpes zoster (unilateral distribution along nerve segments) and contact dermatitis have been excluded

essential: Dermatology specialist visual inspection (typical signs of clustered vesicles on an erythematous base)
if_suspected: Herpesvirus PCR nucleic acid testing or HSV-1/HSV-2 type-specific antibody testing (to confirm viral subtype)
Tzanck cytology smear (scraping the base of a vesicle shows multinucleated giant cells and intranuclear inclusions)
avoid: Abuse of lumbar puncture cerebrospinal fluid examination without signs of central nervous system infection
Abuse of whole-body contrast-enhanced CT or intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics for simple localized labial herpes

first_line: Antiviral therapy: oral acyclovir (200 mg per dose, 5 times daily), valacyclovir (300-500 mg per dose, twice daily), or famciclovir, for 5-10 days
Topical acyclovir cream, penciclovir cream, or calamine lotion
Add mupirocin ointment when secondary bacterial infection occurs.
safety_warnings: Oral antivirals should be started as early as possible within 48 hours of prodromal symptoms or rash for best effect
Patients with renal impairment using acyclovir/valacyclovir require strict dose reduction according to creatinine clearance and adequate hydration to prevent renal tubular crystal injury
Avoid scratching or picking open vesicles at the affected site, and avoid kissing infants to prevent severe neonatal herpes infection
personalization: Frequent recurrent patients (recurrence >=6 times per year): consider oral low-dose valacyclovir or acyclovir suppressive maintenance therapy for 6-12 months
Immunodeficient/HIV patients: lesions tend to be extensive, severe, and necrotic; intravenous acyclovir is required
Genital herpes infection during pregnancy: evaluate delivery mode under close coordination between obstetrics and dermatology to prevent vertical transmission to the newborn through the birth canal

skills.presentation: Patients often report persistent erythema, pustules, and crusting at the tips of the fingers or toes; the lesions are chronic and progressive and tend to recur. Typical features include lesions confined to the periungual or distal areas, with nail bed destruction, nail plate deformity or loss, and secondary bacterial infection often causing local swelling and pain. Lesion borders are well defined and may spread proximally, but other body sites are usually not involved; the course is prolonged and refractory.

first_questions: Which finger or toe did the symptoms first appear on? Is there a history of trauma?
Are the lesions continuously present or do they wax and wane? Have they ever ruptured and drained pus on their own?
Have you ever been diagnosed with psoriasis or eczema? Is there a family history of similar conditions?
followup_questions: If the nails are deformed, is there severe pain or does it interfere with daily grasping?
Have you used topical corticosteroid ointments recently, and did the symptoms change after use?
Do you have a history of diabetes or immune system disease that may affect wound healing?
stop_conditions: The extent of lesion distribution, morphological features, and associated nail changes have been clearly defined.
Obvious systemic infection or other systemic disease triggers have been excluded.
The patient can provide a complete history of prior treatment and allergies.

essential: Dermoscopy
Bacterial and fungal culture
Histopathological examination
if_suspected: Complete blood count and C-reactive protein (to assess infection severity)
Blood glucose testing (to rule out diabetes)
Autoantibody panel (to differentiate autoimmune diseases)
avoid: Whole-body CT scanning without indication
Unnecessary bone marrow aspiration
Long-term combination use of empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics without culture evidence

first_line: First-line treatment is topical potent corticosteroid (e.g., halometasone cream) under occlusion for 4-8 weeks

When infection is present, add mupirocin ointment. For refractory cases, oral retinoids (e.g., acitretin) may be considered at a starting dose of 0.25mg/kg/d, adjusted according to tolerability, with monitoring of lipids and liver function. Also keep the affected area clean and dry and avoid mechanical irritation.
safety_warnings: Long-term use of potent corticosteroids requires vigilance for skin atrophy and telangiectasia
Retinoids are teratogenic; women of childbearing potential must use strict contraception during treatment and for 3 months after discontinuation
Be alert to the risk of drug-induced liver injury and monitor liver function regularly
personalization: In pediatric patients, use a lower corticosteroid concentration and shorter course, and prefer calcineurin inhibitors
Older patients with diabetes require strict glycemic control to prevent secondary severe infection
Retinoids are contraindicated in pregnant women; only short-term, small-area use of low-potency corticosteroids is permitted

skills.presentation: Patients often report generalized unusually light color of the skin, hair, and iris, appearing milky white or pale yellow. Since childhood, they have symptoms such as photophobia, blurred vision, and nystagmus. The skin is extremely sensitive to sunlight; minimal sun exposure can cause severe sunburn, and there is a predisposition to actinic keratosis or skin cancer. Depigmented macules have well-defined borders, and hair is fine, soft, and sparse.

first_questions: Have you or family members noticed unusually light skin and hair color since birth?
Does the child have light sensitivity, blurred vision, or involuntary eye movements?
After sun exposure, does the skin easily become red or blister, or do these changes persist for a long time?
followup_questions: Are there relatives with similar symptoms in the family?
Have eye examinations shown retinal dysplasia or abnormal optic nerve conduction?
Have you had any history of sun-induced precancerous skin lesions or malignant tumors?
stop_conditions: Typical generalized pigment loss in the skin, hair, and eyes has been clearly identified.
Characteristic symptoms such as photophobia and visual impairment have been confirmed.
The family history is highly consistent with the clinical presentation, and no further questioning is needed.

essential: Dermoscopy (to observe hair follicle and epidermal pigment distribution)
Ophthalmologic specialty examination (including fundus photography and visual evoked potential [VEP])
Wood's lamp examination (to help assess the extent of pigment loss)
if_suspected: Genetic testing (e.g., mutation analysis of OCA1-4-related genes)
Skin biopsy (pathological examination to confirm melanocyte loss)
Hearing testing (to rule out comorbidities of Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome)
avoid: Routine skin fungal culture (unnecessary when there is no indication of infection)
Unnecessary whole-body CT or MRI (unless neurologic complications are suspected)
Empirical corticosteroid therapeutic trial (contraindicated when there is no evidence of inflammation)

first_line: There is currently no curative treatment; the core is sun protection and symptomatic management. Strict physical sun protection: wear long-sleeved clothing and a wide-brimmed hat, use broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF50+ and reapply every 2 hours. Ocular intervention: wear UV-blocking sunglasses and, if necessary, provide refractive correction or amblyopia training. Regular dermatologic follow-up to monitor for skin cancer, with early excision of precancerous lesions. Avoid intense light exposure and use UV-blocking curtains indoors.
safety_warnings: Strictly avoid cosmetics or drugs containing photosensitizing ingredients
Avoid self-use of skin-lightening products, which may worsen skin damage
Be alert to the risk of toxicity from long-term high-dose vitamin D supplementation
personalization: Pediatric patients need strengthened guidance on protective measures in the school environment and parental education
Patients with darker skin types still require equivalent sun protection to prevent occult malignant transformation
Patients with a bleeding tendency (e.g., HPS type) should avoid traumatic procedures and undergo coagulation monitoring

skills.presentation: Patients report the sudden appearance of round or oval, smooth, hairless areas on the scalp with well-defined borders; the skin in the lesions is normal, without scaling, redness, swelling, or pain. The alopecic areas may be single or multiple, and in severe cases may progress to loss of all scalp hair (alopecia totalis) or all body hair (alopecia universalis). Some patients have local itching, stinging, or formication before or during hair loss, often triggered or worsened by psychological stress.

first_questions: How long have the hairless areas been present? Did they appear suddenly or gradually enlarge?
Have you recently had major psychological stress, sleep deprivation, or emotional fluctuations?
Is there also hair loss on other body areas (such as eyebrows, beard, or body hair)?
followup_questions: Does the skin in the hairless areas itch, hurt, or burn?
Is there a family history of similar hair loss or autoimmune disease?
Do you have a history of thyroid disease, vitiligo, or allergic disease?
stop_conditions: The hair loss has been clearly identified as typical round patches with no inflammatory skin changes.
Fungal infection (such as tinea capitis) and features of scarring alopecia have been excluded.
Triggers and accompanying symptoms have been clarified sufficiently for a preliminary diagnosis.

essential: Dermoscopy (to observe yellow dot sign, black dot sign, and exclamation mark hairs)
Hair pull test (to assess the degree of active hair loss)
if_suspected: Thyroid function tests (to rule out Hashimoto thyroiditis, etc.)
Autoantibody panel screening (to rule out systemic lupus erythematosus, etc.)
Fungal microscopy and culture (to rule out tinea capitis)
avoid: Routine scalp biopsy (unless scarring alopecia is suspected or the diagnosis is unclear)
Unnecessary whole-body imaging (when there are no systemic symptoms)

first_line: For localized alopecia areata, first-line treatment is topical corticosteroids, such as halometasone cream applied topically once or twice daily, or intralesional triamcinolone acetonide injection every 4 weeks. For rapidly progressive or multiple alopecia areata, topical minoxidil solution may be added to promote regrowth. Non-pharmacologic interventions include psychological counseling to reduce anxiety and ensuring adequate sleep. The general course should last 3-6 months, adjusted according to hair follicle recovery.
safety_warnings: Long-term large-area use of potent corticosteroids may cause skin atrophy and telangiectasia and requires regular monitoring.
Intralesional injection may cause local depression or hypopigmentation; injection depth and dose should be strictly controlled.
Avoid combining with immunosuppressants because of the increased risk of severe infection.
personalization: Use potent corticosteroids with caution in pediatric patients; prefer low-potency agents or calcineurin inhibitors.
Systemic drugs such as methotrexate are contraindicated in pregnant and breastfeeding women; topical treatment should be carefully evaluated.
For patients with alopecia totalis or universalis, early referral to a specialty center is recommended to consider systemic treatment such as JAK inhibitors.

skills.presentation: Patients report diffuse, complete hair loss with a smooth scalp and no signs of inflammation. It usually develops from alopecia areata, and the course may be accompanied by punctate nail pitting or rough nail surface. Some patients may describe recent major psychological stress, sleep disturbance, or a history of autoimmune disease; the alopecic areas are not painful or itchy, but scalp vascular markings may be visibly prominent.

first_questions: Did your hair loss start as localized patches or did all your hair suddenly fall out? How long has it lasted?
Have you recently had major psychological stress, sleep deprivation, or an infection?
Is there a family history of similar hair loss or autoimmune diseases such as thyroid disease?
followup_questions: Have you noticed shedding of eyebrows, eyelashes, or body hair as well?
Are there pinhead-sized pits or transverse grooves on the nail surface?
Is there currently redness, swelling, scaling, or pain on the scalp?
stop_conditions: Complete loss of all scalp hair has been clearly identified, and features of scarring alopecia have been excluded.
There is no confirmed active infection or symptoms of severe systemic disease.
The patient has provided complete information on prior treatment history and family history.

essential: Dermoscopy (to observe yellow and black dot signs and exclamation mark hairs)
Hair pull test
Thyroid function and antibody tests
if_suspected: Serum ferritin and vitamin D level measurement
Antinuclear antibody panel screening
Scalp biopsy (if scarring alopecia is suspected or in atypical cases)
avoid: Routine fungal culture (not caused by fungal infection)
Unnecessary whole-body CT or MRI examinations
Excessive imaging workup before empirical pulse corticosteroid therapy

first_line: First-line treatment is topical potent corticosteroids (e.g., halometasone cream) applied once or twice daily for at least 3 months

Combine with 5% minoxidil tincture to promote hair follicle regeneration. For rapidly progressive cases, intralesional triamcinolone acetonide injection may be considered every 4 weeks. Psychological counseling is also recommended to prevent anxiety from worsening the condition.
safety_warnings: Long-term large-area use of potent corticosteroids requires vigilance for skin atrophy, telangiectasia, and secondary infection.
Corticosteroid injections require strict aseptic technique to prevent subcutaneous fat atrophy and depigmentation.
Systemic immunosuppressants are contraindicated in pregnant and breastfeeding women; topical medications should be carefully evaluated.
personalization: For pediatric patients, prefer low-potency corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors to avoid affecting growth and development.
Older patients require monitoring of blood pressure and blood glucose, and systemic drugs should be used with caution.
Patients with concomitant thyroid disease need concurrent endocrinology treatment to improve prognosis.

skills.presentation: Patients often report severe itching of the feet, especially at night or after removing shoes. Typical signs include macerated, whitened skin between the toes with erosion and exudation, or dry scaling, hyperkeratosis, and fissuring on the soles. Some patients may have vesicles that rupture to form annular scales. If secondary bacterial infection occurs, redness, swelling, warmth, pain, and purulent discharge may be present.

first_questions: Where exactly on your feet is the itching? Have you noticed any blisters or peeling?
How long have your symptoms lasted? Do they recur?
followup_questions: Do you have a history of diabetes or a weakened immune system?
Has anyone else in your household had similar symptoms? Do you usually share slippers or towels?
stop_conditions: Typical skin lesion features (such as interdigital maceration or scaling) have been clearly described, and there are no severe systemic symptoms.
It has been confirmed that there is no underlying disease such as diabetes that could interfere with diagnosis.
The patient has provided recent medication history and allergy history.

essential: Fungal microscopy (KOH mount)
Wood's lamp examination (adjunctive differential diagnosis)
if_suspected: Fungal culture (for refractory or recurrent cases)
Bacterial culture (when concurrent bacterial infection is suspected)
avoid: Routine X-ray examination (no indication)
Unnecessary systemic corticosteroid therapeutic trial

first_line: First-line treatment is topical antifungal agents, such as bifonazole cream or terbinafine cream, applied once or twice daily for at least 2-4 weeks; after symptoms resolve, continue treatment for 1 week to prevent recurrence. Keep the feet dry and clean, and wear breathable shoes and socks. If bacterial infection is present, mupirocin ointment may be used in combination.
safety_warnings: Avoid long-term use of potent corticosteroid combination products over large areas to prevent tinea incognito.
Contraindicated in patients allergic to imidazoles or allylamines.
Pregnant and breastfeeding women should use topical drugs cautiously under medical supervision.
personalization: Patients with diabetes need strict blood glucose monitoring and enhanced foot care to prevent ulcers.
For patients with hyperkeratotic disease, salicylic acid ointment may be used first to soften keratin, followed by antifungal agents.
For pediatric patients, choose formulations with low irritation and avoid high-concentration products.

skills.presentation: Patients report a distinctive pungent odor in the axillae, resembling unripe fruit or onions, which worsens in summer or after sweating during exercise. It is often accompanied by yellowing and stiffening of clothing (especially in the axillary area) due to sweat staining. Some patients develop social anxiety because of the odor and deliberately avoid raising their arms or close contact with others. Symptoms usually begin in puberty and may lessen with age.

first_questions: Have you noticed a distinctive pungent odor in your axillae when you sweat?
Does this odor become noticeably worse in summer, during exercise, or when you are emotionally stressed?
Do any of your first-degree relatives have a similar condition?
followup_questions: If the odor affects your social life, how long has this been going on?
Have you tried antiperspirants, shaving your axillary hair, or other methods to relieve it? How effective were they?
Is there any redness, swelling, pain, or discharge in the axillary skin that might indicate infection?
stop_conditions: The onset time, triggers, and family history have been clearly obtained, and there are no signs of acute infection.
The patient has described typical symptoms and expressed a desire for treatment, and no further differential diagnosis is needed.
When conservative non-surgical treatment has been ineffective and the patient is being prepared for surgical evaluation.

essential: Inspection: observe axillary skin color and the presence of pigmentation or scarring.
Palpation: examine the areas of apocrine gland distribution in the axilla and press to check for discharge.
Iodine-starch test: used to locate areas of active apocrine secretion.
if_suspected: Bacterial culture: if concurrent bacterial infection is suspected to be worsening the odor.
Dermoscopy: to exclude other skin lesions such as early manifestations of hidradenitis suppurativa.
avoid: Routine complete blood count (when there is no indication of infection).
Hormone level testing (unless secondary hyperhidrosis due to endocrine disease is suspected).

first_line: First-line treatment is topical agents, such as 20% aluminum chloride solution or antiperspirants containing triclosan/antibacterial ingredients, applied to dry axillae every night before bedtime for 2-4 weeks. Combine with local shaving of axillary hair to reduce bacterial growth. If ineffective, botulinum toxin injection (50-100 units per side) may be considered, with effects lasting 6-9 months. For severe cases, minimally invasive curettage or laser treatment to destroy apocrine glands is recommended.
safety_warnings: Aluminum chloride preparations may cause contact dermatitis; if redness, swelling, or itching occurs, discontinue immediately and apply cold compresses.
Botulinum toxin injection should avoid areas with dense nerves and blood vessels to prevent upper limb weakness.
Improper surgery may lead to subcutaneous hematoma, hypertrophic scarring, or compensatory hyperhidrosis.
personalization: For adolescent patients, conservative treatment is recommended first, and surgery should be evaluated after adulthood.
Use excisional surgery cautiously in patients prone to scarring; laser or radiofrequency ablation is recommended.
Botulinum toxin and certain oral medications are contraindicated in pregnant and breastfeeding women; only physical care is recommended.

skills.presentation: Patients often report severe itching followed by tense bullae, predominantly on the flexural aspects of the limbs and the abdomen. The lesions have an obviously erythematous base, the blisters do not rupture easily, and the Nikolsky sign is negative. Some patients initially have only urticarial or eczematous eruptions, which are easily misdiagnosed. It occurs mainly in older adults, has a chronic course, and may involve mucous membranes, although this is less common.

first_questions: Have you had unbearable itching on your body?
Have you recently developed blisters on your skin, and do they rupture easily?
followup_questions: On which parts of your body do the blisters mainly appear?
Did you take any new medications (such as diuretics or glucose-lowering drugs) before the onset?
stop_conditions: Typical itching and tense bulla features have been clearly described.
It has been confirmed that there is no history of new drug exposure and that symptoms persist.
Other common triggers of blistering skin disease have been excluded.

essential: Skin histopathology examination
Direct immunofluorescence (DIF)
if_suspected: Indirect immunofluorescence (IIF)
Serum anti-BP180/BP230 antibody testing
avoid: Routine bacterial culture (unless there is clear evidence of secondary infection)
Non-indicated tests before empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy

first_line: First-line treatment is a potent topical corticosteroid (such as clobetasol), applied once daily to the whole body or affected areas, then gradually tapered after a 4-6 week course. For severe or extensive lesions, oral prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day is given as a single morning dose and slowly tapered after disease control. Combination with doxycycline may reduce the corticosteroid dose. Combine with moisturizing skin care and antipruritic treatment.
safety_warnings: Long-term corticosteroid use requires vigilance for hyperglycemia, hypertension, and osteoporosis.
Avoid abrupt discontinuation, which may cause disease rebound.
Monitor for the risk of secondary fungal or bacterial infection.
personalization: For elderly patients, the starting dose should be low, with close monitoring of metabolic parameters.
Patients with diabetes require intensified blood glucose monitoring and adjustment of glucose-lowering regimens.
Use doxycycline cautiously in patients with renal impairment; prefer corticosteroid monotherapy or rituximab.

skills.presentation: Patients report flat macules ranging from light brown to dark brown, with clear borders, irregular shapes, and variable sizes. They commonly occur on the trunk, limbs, or face and are usually asymptomatic, neither painful nor itchy. If the number of macules increases or the diameter exceeds a certain range (e.g., >5 mm before puberty), genetic diseases such as neurofibromatosis should be considered.

first_questions: When were these spots first noticed? Have they been gradually increasing in number?
Does anyone in your family have similar skin findings or other related diseases?
followup_questions: If there are many spots, are they accompanied by other symptoms such as subcutaneous nodules, vision problems, or skeletal abnormalities?
Do the spots darken after sun exposure or become itchy?
stop_conditions: It has been clearly established as an isolated café-au-lait macule, with no family history or other symptoms.
The patient's treatment need is only cosmetic improvement, and no further examination is required.
The necessary physical examination and history taking have been completed.

essential: Wood's lamp examination
Dermoscopy
if_suspected: Genetic testing (e.g., NF1 gene)
Neurological imaging (MRI)
avoid: Skin biopsy (unless malignancy is suspected)
Routine blood tests (no specific markers)

first_line: There is currently no specific drug treatment for café-au-lait macules. For patients concerned about appearance, laser therapy (such as Q-switched laser or picosecond laser) may be considered, usually requiring multiple sessions. Non-pharmacological interventions include sun protection to reduce worsening of pigmentation.
safety_warnings: Avoid unproven home remedies or potent bleaching agents.
Hypopigmentation or scarring may occur after laser treatment; strict sun protection is required.
Use laser treatment cautiously during pregnancy.
personalization: For pediatric patients, carefully assess the necessity and risks of treatment.
For individuals with darker skin, choose laser parameters more cautiously to avoid pigmentary abnormalities.
In patients with neurofibromatosis, the primary disease should be treated first.

skills.presentation: Patients often report hard, irregular nodules or plaques on the skin, which feel stone-like on palpation; the overlying skin may appear white or yellowish-white. They commonly occur on pressure-bearing areas such as the fingers, elbows, and knees. Some cases are accompanied by local redness, swelling, pain, or ulceration with discharge of chalky material. When associated with systemic sclerosis, joint stiffness and Raynaud phenomenon are often present.

first_questions: How long have you noticed the skin lumps? Have they gradually enlarged or become harder?
Are the lumps accompanied by pain, redness, swelling, or ulceration with discharge?
Do you have a history of rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis, or thyroid disease?
followup_questions: Have you recently had trauma, injected drugs, or exposure to chemicals?
Has the skin color around the lumps changed, and is there any abnormal sensation or limitation of movement?
Is there a family history of similar skin disease or autoimmune disease?
stop_conditions: The history, symptom characteristics, and underlying diseases have been clarified, and there are no new warning symptoms.
The patient has provided a complete medication history and allergy history sufficient to assess treatment risk.
The clinical presentation is typical, the initial differential diagnosis is clear, and no further detailed questioning is needed.

essential: Plain radiography of the skin and soft tissues (to confirm the morphology and distribution of calcifications)
High-frequency ultrasonography (to assess the depth of calcification and surrounding tissue inflammation)
Serum calcium, phosphorus, and parathyroid hormone levels (to evaluate metabolic causes)
if_suspected: Antinuclear antibody panel and ENA antibody testing (to evaluate connective tissue disease)
Dual-energy CT scanning (for precise quantification of calcium deposition and compositional analysis)
Skin biopsy with pathologic examination (to confirm the type and exclude neoplastic calcification)
avoid: Routine complete blood count (no direct specific value for determining the nature of calcification)
Unnecessary whole-body bone scan (unless widespread bone metastases or metabolic abnormalities are suspected)
Empiric antibiotic therapy (ineffective for noninfectious lesions and increases the risk of resistance)

first_line: First-line treatment focuses on controlling the underlying disease and relieving symptoms. Mild asymptomatic cases can be observed periodically.

For symptomatic patients, topical dimethyl sulfoxide ointment or oral calcium channel blockers such as diltiazem or verapamil can be used to reduce calcium deposition. For localized refractory lesions, surgical excision or laser therapy may be considered. Serum calcium and phosphorus levels should also be strictly managed, and a high-calcium diet should be avoided.
safety_warnings: Monitor blood pressure when using calcium channel blockers to prevent hypotension.
Coagulation function must be assessed before surgical excision to prevent postoperative bleeding and infection.
Avoid blind needle aspiration to prevent secondary infection or worsening of tissue damage.
personalization: Use phosphate binders with caution in patients with renal impairment, and adjust the dose.
For elderly patients, surgical healing capacity should be carefully assessed, and minimally invasive approaches should be preferred.
Retinoids are contraindicated in pregnant women, and treatment must balance fetal safety.

skills.presentation: Patients often report yellowing of the skin, most prominent on the palms, soles, and nasolabial folds. The sclerae are usually not icteric, which is the key distinction from jaundice. The skin is orange-yellow or lemon-yellow, without inflammatory manifestations such as pruritus or scaling. Symptoms are often related to recent high intake of carotene-rich foods (such as carrots, pumpkin, and oranges), and the color may gradually fade after discontinuation.

first_questions: Have you recently eaten large amounts of foods such as carrots, pumpkin, oranges, or mangoes?
Besides yellowing of the skin, are the sclerae of your eyes also yellow?
followup_questions: How long has this skin color change been present? Does it coincide with changes in your diet?
Do you have other symptoms such as fatigue, decreased appetite, or dark urine?
stop_conditions: It is confirmed that the sclerae are not icteric and the skin shows only orange-yellow changes
There is a clear history of recent high intake of carotene-rich foods
Typical symptoms of liver dysfunction and hemolytic disease have been excluded

essential: Serum total bilirubin measurement
Comprehensive liver function tests
if_suspected: Complete blood count (to exclude hemolytic anemia)
Thyroid function tests (to exclude metabolic abnormalities caused by hypothyroidism)
avoid: Skin biopsy (this condition is benign pigmentation and does not require pathologic confirmation)
Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT (unnecessary when there is no indication of organic disease)

first_line: This condition is self-limited and requires no specific drug therapy. The core measure is to adjust the diet and reduce intake of fruits and vegetables rich in β-carotene (such as carrots, pumpkin, and citrus fruits). It is usually recommended to suspend the relevant foods for 2-6 weeks; after carotene is metabolized and cleared from the body, the skin yellowing may resolve spontaneously. Patients should also be encouraged to drink more water to promote metabolism.
safety_warnings: Do not blindly use drugs to reduce yellowing or steroid therapy, as this may mask the true condition
Be alert to misdiagnosing this condition as hepatitis and providing unnecessary hepatoprotective treatment
Long-term excessive intake may cause gastrointestinal discomfort; attention should be paid to a balanced diet
personalization: Infants and young children: feeding plans should be assessed, and overreliance on carrot puree as a single complementary food should be avoided
Patients with diabetes: while limiting high-sugar fruits, ensure nutritional supplementation with alternative vegetables
Older adults: evaluate whether hypothyroidism is causing slowed metabolism

skills.presentation: Patients often report localized purplish-red swellings on distal areas such as the hands, feet, and auricles after exposure to cold, damp environments, accompanied by a marked sensation of swelling. Typical symptoms include localized coldness and numbness of the skin, with severe pruritus or burning pain upon warming; severe cases may develop vesicles, ulcers, and secondary infection. Lesions are often symmetrically distributed, occur most frequently in winter, and resolve spontaneously in spring but tend to recur.

first_questions: Before the symptoms appeared, had you been exposed to cold, damp environments for a prolonged period?
At the affected area, is the main sensation currently itching, pain, or numbness?
followup_questions: If vesicles or ulceration have developed, is there any discharge or sign of fever?
In previous years, have you had similar symptoms in the same season or at the same site?
stop_conditions: A history of cold exposure is clear, and typical skin lesions (purplish-red swelling) are evident.
It has been confirmed that there is no systemic circulatory disorder (such as Raynaud disease or lupus erythematosus).
Secondary bacterial infection or necrosis has been excluded.

essential: Inspection: observe the morphology and color of the lesions and the presence of vesicles/ulcers
Palpation: assess skin temperature, degree of swelling, and tenderness
if_suspected: Complete blood count: to evaluate secondary infection or hematologic abnormalities
Autoantibody panel: to differentiate acral vascular lesions caused by connective tissue disease
Nailfold microcirculation examination: to assess peripheral blood circulation
avoid: Unnecessary X-ray examination (unless concomitant fracture or periostitis is suspected)
Routine bacterial culture (perform only when purulent infection is evident)
Invasive biopsy (pathologic confirmation is not needed in typical cases)

first_line: First-line treatment focuses on improving local blood circulation and reducing inflammation. Apply topical 10% camphor ointment or heparin sodium cream 2-3 times daily to promote reduction of swelling and relieve pain.

If vesicles are present, they may be aspirated aseptically, followed by topical antibiotic ointment to prevent infection. Oral nifedipine sustained-release tablets (30 mg qd) can dilate blood vessels; the course is about 2-4 weeks. Also emphasize keeping warm and dry, avoid alternating cold and heat stimulation, and strictly prohibit direct exposure to fire or soaking the affected area in hot water.
safety_warnings: Do not allow overheated objects to contact the affected area directly, to prevent burns that may worsen tissue damage
Nifedipine may cause hypotension or facial flushing; blood pressure should be monitored
Camphor-containing preparations are contraindicated in patients allergic to camphor and should be used with caution in pregnant women
personalization: Reduce doses in children, and prefer gentle topical moisturizers
In older adults, monitor blood pressure changes and adjust the calcium channel blocker dose
In patients with diabetes, strictly monitor wound healing to prevent diabetic foot complications

skills.presentation: Patients often develop pinhead- to millet-sized wheals within minutes after exercise, heat exposure, emotional excitement, or eating spicy foods, surrounded by marked erythema. The typical complaint is severe pruritus, stinging, or burning over the whole body or the upper trunk; lesions usually resolve spontaneously within 30-60 minutes without leaving marks. Some patients may have systemic symptoms such as headache, salivation, abdominal pain, or dyspnea.

first_questions: Do the symptoms appear rapidly after exercise, a hot bath, or emotional stress?
Are the rashes accompanied by marked stinging or burning rather than simple itching?
How long does each episode last, and do the symptoms resolve spontaneously after resting and cooling down?
followup_questions: If you have palpitations or shortness of breath, have you ever had laryngeal edema or syncope?
If food is suspected as a trigger, was the specific food you ate spicy or hot?
If conventional antihistamines are ineffective, have you recently changed medications or do you have other concurrent diseases?
stop_conditions: The trigger and typical lesion features (small wheals + erythema + stinging itch) are clear, and there is no severe systemic allergic reaction.
The history is clear, and there are previous episodes that resolved spontaneously.
Physical examination shows typical induced lesions, and no further complex questioning is needed.

essential: Dermatographism test (to exclude other physical urticarias)
Provocation test (e.g., induced by exercise or a hot bath)
Complete blood count and IgE level testing
if_suspected: Intradermal acetylcholine injection test (when diagnosis is difficult)
Thyroid function and autoantibody screening (to evaluate autoimmune factors)
Electrocardiographic monitoring (if accompanied by palpitations or presyncope)
avoid: Blind comprehensive food allergen screening (unless a clear dietary association is established)
Repeated unnecessary imaging studies
Complex immunologic testing before steroid pulse therapy in the absence of an indication

first_line: First-line treatment is a second-generation nonsedating antihistamine, such as cetirizine 10 mg once daily or loratadine 10 mg once daily. If the standard dose is ineffective, it may be increased to 2-4 times the dose under medical supervision. Nonpharmacologic interventions include avoiding strenuous exercise, hot environments, and spicy foods. The course is usually 2-4 weeks, with gradual dose reduction and discontinuation according to symptom control.
safety_warnings: Avoid concomitant use with alcohol or other central nervous system depressants to prevent worsening drowsiness
Use with caution in patients with hepatic impairment, and adjust the dose
Be alert to the rare risk of arrhythmia, especially with high-dose use
personalization: In children, calculate the dose by body weight; it is usually halved or as directed by a physician
For pregnant and breastfeeding women, loratadine or cetirizine is preferred, with the benefits and risks weighed
In older adults, consider the effect of reduced renal function on drug metabolism, and use a low starting dose

skills.presentation: The patient complains that sweat is abnormally colored (e.g., yellow, green, blue, black, etc.) rather than normal colorless and transparent. Symptoms usually appear when sweating and commonly involve the face, axillae, or trunk; sweat may stain clothing or skin. Some patients have an odor, but severe pain or systemic discomfort is usually absent; symptoms worsen only under specific emotional stress or high-temperature environments.

first_questions: What color exactly is your sweat? Is it persistent or occasional?
Which parts of the body are mainly affected by this discoloration? Is it accompanied by staining of clothing?
Have you recently changed to new skincare products or medications, or eaten any special foods?
followup_questions: Is the discolored area accompanied by symptoms such as itching, pain, or rash?
Do symptoms worsen after contact with specific chemicals or metals?
Is there a family history of similar conditions or inherited metabolic diseases?
stop_conditions: The color characteristics, distribution, and triggering factors of the sweat have been clarified.
Pseudochromhidrosis caused by exogenous pigment exposure (e.g., hair dye, dyes) has been excluded.
It has been confirmed that there are no signs of other systemic infections or severe skin lesions.

essential: Wood's lamp examination
Sweat bacterial culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing
Dermoscopy
if_suspected: Fungal microscopy and culture (to exclude fungal infection)
Serum ceruloplasmin assay (to rule out Wilson disease)
Histopathological biopsy (for difficult cases)
avoid: Unnecessary comprehensive systemic blood biochemistry screening
Excessive testing before non-targeted empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy
Radionuclide scanning without indication

first_line: First-line treatment is topical antibacterials (e.g., erythromycin ointment, clindamycin gel) twice daily for 2-4 weeks to inhibit pigment-producing bacteria. If caused by exogenous pigments, discontinue the relevant contactant and enhance local cleaning. For refractory cases, benzoyl peroxide wash or low-concentration salicylic acid preparations may be used in combination. Also instruct the patient to keep the affected area dry and avoid friction from tight clothing.
safety_warnings: Avoid long-term, large-area use of potent corticosteroid ointments to prevent skin atrophy.
Be aware that topical antibiotics may cause contact dermatitis or resistance.
If the patient is allergic to quinolones or macrolides, the corresponding drugs are contraindicated.
personalization: For pediatric patients, prioritize gentle physical cleansing methods and use high-concentration chemical preparations with caution.
Pregnant and breastfeeding women should avoid tetracyclines and quinolones.
Older adults have impaired skin barrier function; reduce drug concentration and shorten the treatment course.

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of chronic nonhealing verrucous or cauliflower-like proliferative skin lesions on exposed areas such as the feet and lower legs, with a rough surface and crusting, and possible chronic ulcers and fistulas. The course persists for years; initially small papules gradually enlarge and coalesce into plaques, with the border elevated in a dike-like pattern and the center tending to heal. Some patients have a history of trauma (e.g., walking barefoot and being punctured by a wooden splinter). Regional lymph nodes may be enlarged, but systemic symptoms are usually mild.

first_questions: Where did the skin lesion first appear? Have you ever walked barefoot in soil or been punctured by a plant thorn?
How long has this wound or lump been present? Has it recently enlarged or become ulcerated with pus drainage?
followup_questions: If the patient mentions pain or itching, ask further: 'Is the pain continuous, or does it worsen only when touched?'
If lymph node enlargement is noted, ask: 'Have you felt enlarged hard lumps in the neck or groin? Is it accompanied by fever?'
stop_conditions: The lesion morphology has been clarified as verrucous proliferation with a course of more than 6 months, and a history of soil contact has been confirmed.
The patient has described the typical features of biphasic lesions (central healing and active borders).
Other fungal infections or skin tumors have been preliminarily excluded.

essential: Microscopic examination of skin scrapings (KOH wet mount) for thick-walled spores (Medlar bodies)
Fungal culture to identify the causative species
Skin biopsy for pathological examination (to observe granulomas and pigmented hyphae)
if_suspected: Special histopathological stains (PAS stain, methenamine silver stain)
Molecular biological testing (PCR) to distinguish mixed infections
Chest X-ray or CT (to exclude extrapulmonary dissemination)
avoid: Empiric use of broad-spectrum antibiotics (when there is no evidence of bacterial infection)
Unnecessary deep needle biopsy (which may easily lead to secondary infection)
Routine bacterial culture (not the primary target of evaluation)

first_line: First-line treatment is oral itraconazole at 200-400 mg/day for at least 6-12 months, continuing consolidation treatment for 3-6 months after clinical cure. For localized lesions, local cryotherapy or surgical excision may be combined. For severe or refractory cases, intravenous amphotericin B or combination with flucytosine may be considered. The affected area should also be kept clean and dry, and trauma should be avoided.
safety_warnings: Itraconazole is hepatotoxic; liver function should be monitored regularly before and during treatment.
The drug interacts with many medications (e.g., statins, warfarin); medication history should be carefully reviewed.
Itraconazole should be used with caution in patients with cardiac insufficiency because it may precipitate heart failure.
personalization: Pediatric patients require weight-based dose adjustment and close monitoring of growth and development.
Itraconazole is contraindicated in pregnant and breastfeeding women; physical therapy or specialist consultation is recommended instead.
Older adults have slowed metabolism; start with a low dose and be alert to the risk of drug accumulation.

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of painless warty growths on the genitals or perianal area; initially pale red papules that gradually enlarge and increase in number, and may be papillary, cauliflower-like, or cockscomb-like. Some patients have local itching, a foreign-body sensation, or postcoital bleeding. The lesions have a rough, uneven surface, are moist and prone to erosion, and if secondarily infected may have foul-smelling discharge.

first_questions: How long have you had the warty growths on the genitals or perianal area? Have they recently enlarged or increased in number?
In the past 6 months, have you had unprotected sex or a new partner?
followup_questions: Are the warty growths accompanied by itching, pain, or contact bleeding?
Have you had similar conditions in the past or received related treatment?
stop_conditions: Typical lesion morphology and distribution have been clearly described, and there are no complex complications.
The patient has provided a clear sexual history and prior treatment history sufficient to support a preliminary diagnosis.
The patient declines further examination exposing private areas, but the symptom description is highly typical.

essential: Acetowhite test
Dermoscopy
Pathological tissue biopsy (for atypical or refractory cases)
if_suspected: HPV DNA genotyping
Treponema pallidum serologic testing
HIV antibody testing
avoid: Routine chest X-ray (when there is no pulmonary indication)
Unnecessary whole-body CT scanning
Nonspecific inflammatory marker screening (e.g., CRP) if there are no signs of infection

first_line: First-line treatment is physical therapy such as cryotherapy or laser removal of visible warts. Topical options include 5% imiquimod cream (applied 3 times per week at bedtime and washed off after 6-10 hours) or podophyllotoxin tincture (twice daily, 3 days on and 4 days off). The course usually lasts several weeks until the warts completely resolve, and follow-up observation for 3 months is recommended to prevent recurrence. Health education should also be provided, and sexual contact should be avoided until recovery.
safety_warnings: Podophyllotoxin is contraindicated in pregnant women and on broken mucosa to avoid severe tissue necrosis.
Imiquimod may cause local redness, swelling, and ulceration; patients should be instructed on the correct application area.
During treatment, patients must not scratch or squeeze the warts themselves to prevent viral spread.
personalization: For pregnant women, cryotherapy or surgical excision is preferred; podophyllotoxin and imiquimod are contraindicated.
Immunosuppressed patients require a longer course and close monitoring for recurrence.
For pediatric patients, use caustic drugs with caution and prioritize physical therapy.

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of purpura, livedo reticularis, or ulcers on both lower limbs after cold exposure, accompanied by joint pain and fatigue. The typical presentation is that skin lesions worsen after cold exposure and improve in a warm environment. Some patients have Raynaud phenomenon, digital necrosis, or mucosal petechiae. Symptoms have a clear seasonal or ambient temperature dependence, and the possibility of coexisting liver disease (e.g., hepatitis C) or an autoimmune disease background should be considered.

first_questions: Do your skin rashes worsen significantly with contact with cold water or cold air, or in winter?
Do you have joint pain, muscle weakness, or unexplained fever?
Do you have a history of hepatitis B or hepatitis C, or long-term alcohol use?
followup_questions: If your fingertips turn white, then purple, then red, does that suggest Raynaud phenomenon?
Have you recently had changes in urine color (e.g., tea-colored urine) or frothy urine?
Have you ever been diagnosed with an autoimmune disease (e.g., Sjögren syndrome)?
stop_conditions: The causal relationship between the rash and cold exposure and the typical distribution have been clarified.
Key history of underlying diseases (e.g., viral hepatitis, autoimmune disease) has been obtained.
It has been confirmed that there is no severe organ involvement (e.g., renal failure, neurologic symptoms).

essential: Serum cryoglobulin quantification
Complement C4 level measurement
Hepatitis C virus antibody and RNA testing
if_suspected: ANA panel and rheumatoid factor testing
Renal function and urinalysis
Immunofluorescence staining of skin biopsy
avoid: Whole-body CT scanning without indication
Unnecessary bone marrow aspiration
Anticoagulation before assessment of coagulation function

first_line: The primary treatment is antiviral therapy for the underlying disease (e.g., hepatitis C). For symptomatic cutaneous vasculitis, first-line regimens include glucocorticoids (prednisone 0.5-1 mg/kg/day) combined with rituximab (375 mg/m² once weekly for 4 doses). At the same time, strictly avoid cold exposure and keep the limbs warm. The treatment course is adjusted according to disease control; glucocorticoids are usually tapered gradually, and biologic therapy is maintained for 6-12 months.
safety_warnings: When using glucocorticoids, monitor blood glucose, blood pressure, and osteoporosis risk.
Rituximab may cause infusion reactions and an increased risk of infection.
Immunosuppressants must not be used when active infection has not been excluded.
personalization: Older patients require a lower starting dose of glucocorticoids and strengthened fall-prevention measures.
Patients with renal insufficiency require dose adjustment based on creatinine clearance.
Rituximab is contraindicated in pregnant women; hydroxychloroquine or low-dose glucocorticoids are preferred.

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of severe itching, stinging, or a sensation of worms moving in the affected area, with local redness, swelling, painful nodules, or ulcers. Typical manifestations include secretions draining from the wound or hair follicles, and sometimes white or milky-white larvae can be directly observed moving under the skin; some cases have a foul odor. Symptoms mostly occur in exposed areas such as the scalp, limbs, or trunk, and the course progresses rapidly; if not treated promptly, tissue necrosis can occur.

first_questions: Do you feel something moving or crawling under your skin?
Have you recently been to the outdoors, farms, or fly-infested environments with poor sanitation?
followup_questions: Is there pus draining from the affected area, or have you seen small white worms emerge?
Before symptoms appeared, was there any history of trauma or insect bite?
stop_conditions: The patient has clearly described seeing larvae or confirmed expulsion of the organism.
History taking has covered epidemiological exposure history and the signs are typical.
The patient has undergone initial debridement and is confirmed to have no other systemic symptoms.

essential: Physical examination (inspection and palpation)
Microscopic examination of lesion secretion smear
Ultrasound (to locate deep larvae)
if_suspected: Complete blood count (to assess infection severity and eosinophils)
Bacterial culture (to exclude secondary bacterial infection)
MRI (for deep tissue involvement)
avoid: Blind incision and drainage (may lead to larval spread or retention)
Routine single-agent antibiotic therapy (cannot kill the parasite)
Direct squeezing without anesthesia (may easily cause larval breakage or rupture)

first_line: First-line physical removal: under local anesthesia, use sterile instruments to remove the larvae completely, avoiding crushing the larval body and causing an allergic reaction. For deep or multiple lesions, first cover the lesion with petrolatum, liquid paraffin, or chloroform to seal the air pores and force the larvae to surface, then remove them. After the procedure, disinfect with povidone-iodine and, depending on the situation, give short-term oral antibiotics to prevent secondary infection. The course depends on the completeness of removal; usually a single treatment is sufficient, with follow-up to observe for recurrence.
safety_warnings: It is strictly forbidden to forcefully squeeze the larvae without anesthesia, to prevent the release of toxins from their body and severe anaphylactic shock.
The procedure must be strictly aseptic to prevent secondary bacterial infection from worsening the condition.
Contraindicated in patients allergic to chloroform and other sealing agents; perform the procedure in a well-ventilated area to prevent inhalation poisoning.
personalization: Pediatric patients require enhanced sedation measures to ensure safe cooperation.
Immunodeficient patients require a prolonged anti-infection observation period and vigilance for sepsis risk.
Pregnant women should use systemic anthelmintic drugs with caution, prioritizing physical removal and local sealing therapy.

skills.presentation: Patients complain of deep, markedly tender red indurated nodules or pustules on the face, chest, and back, often with severe pain. Lesions may coalesce into large plaques and tend to leave depressed scars or hypertrophic scars after healing. Often accompanied by seborrhea; the course is chronic and relapsing, and ordinary topical medications are not effective.

first_questions: How long have these red, swollen, painful lumps been present? Do they recur in the same area?
Do you currently have systemic symptoms such as fever or joint pain?
Have you recently squeezed the lesions yourself, or what medications have you used for treatment?
followup_questions: If the lesions are fluctuant or have ruptured and are draining pus, ask: 'Is there pus accumulation or any sign of secondary infection?'
If scarring is mentioned, ask: 'Do you have a history of severe keloid tendency or keloids?'
If the patient is female, ask: 'Is the worsening of the rash related to the menstrual cycle, and do you have hirsutism or irregular menstruation?'
stop_conditions: The lesion morphology has been clearly identified as deep nodules/cysts, and other inflammatory skin diseases have been excluded.
A complete medication history, allergy history, and record of prior treatment response have been obtained.
Clues to systemic disease (e.g., hormonal abnormalities) have been assessed, and further testing has been decided.

essential: Dermatologic physical examination (inspection and palpation to assess lesion depth, extent, and scarring)
Wood's lamp examination (to help differentiate folliculitis or other pigmentary changes)
Bacterial culture and susceptibility testing when necessary (for recurrent infection or resistance)
if_suspected: Sex hormone panel (to screen for endocrine factors such as polycystic ovary syndrome)
Complete blood count and C-reactive protein (to assess the degree of systemic inflammatory response)
Dermoscopy (to observe follicular plugging and inflammatory features)
avoid: Routine whole-body imaging without indication (e.g., CT/MRI)
Blind incision and drainage of undiagnosed cysts (likely to enlarge scars)
Overreliance on fungal smear examination (unless concurrent fungal infection is highly suspected)

first_line: First-line treatment is oral isotretinoin, starting at 0.25-0.5mg/kg/d, gradually increased to 1mg/kg/d according to tolerability; the course is usually 4-6 months until the lesions completely resolve. Combine with topical benzoyl peroxide or adapalene gel to control surface inflammation. Long-term antibiotic monotherapy is strictly prohibited. Nonpharmacologic interventions include avoiding squeezing, sun protection, and psychological counseling.
safety_warnings: Absolute contraindication: contraindicated during pregnancy in women of childbearing potential; strict contraception is required for at least 3 months before and after treatment.
Drug interactions: combination with tetracycline antibiotics is strictly prohibited to prevent the risk of increased intracranial pressure.
Prevention of serious adverse reactions: regularly monitor liver function and blood lipids, and watch for depressive mood changes and mucosal dryness such as chapped lips.
personalization: Adolescent patients should start at a low dose, with close monitoring of growth and development and epiphyseal closure.
Patients with hepatic or renal impairment require dose reduction or are contraindicated, with increased monitoring frequency.
Patients with a keloid tendency should start anti-scar treatment as early as possible, with local intralesional injection if necessary.

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of intense pruritus, with a symmetric rash that favors the elbows, knees, scapular area, and buttocks. Lesions present as polymorphic papules, vesicles, or bullae on an erythematous base and tend to rupture and crust. Some patients have gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal pain and diarrhea; underlying celiac disease should be considered.

first_questions: Do you have areas of intense itching? Where exactly?
Does the rash appear symmetrically? Are there blisters or ruptures?
followup_questions: Do you have abdominal pain, diarrhea, or other gastrointestinal discomfort?
Is there a family history of similar skin disease or autoimmune disease?
stop_conditions: The rash distribution characteristics and associated symptoms have been clearly defined.
The patient's description is consistent with the typical clinical presentation, and there is no indication of other systemic disease.
Initial history taking has been completed, and skin biopsy is planned.

essential: Skin histopathology (direct immunofluorescence for IgA deposition)
Serum anti-tissue transglutaminase antibody testing
Complete blood count and liver and kidney function tests
if_suspected: Small intestinal mucosal biopsy to evaluate for celiac disease
Thyroid function tests
Vitamin B12 and folate level measurement
avoid: Unnecessary whole-body imaging
Nonspecific allergen screening
Bacterial culture before empiric antibiotic therapy

first_line: First-line treatment is dapsone, starting at 50-100mg/day and adjusted to a maintenance dose according to efficacy. A strict gluten-free diet for at least 6 months is also recommended. Nonpharmacologic interventions include avoiding scratching and keeping the skin clean and dry. The course usually needs to continue for several months until symptoms completely resolve.
safety_warnings: G6PD activity should be tested before treatment to prevent hemolytic reaction
Monitor liver function and hematologic abnormalities
Avoid combination with monoamine oxidase inhibitors
personalization: Elderly patients require dose reduction and close monitoring for adverse reactions
Use with caution in pregnant women; decide the treatment plan after weighing risks and benefits
Pediatric patients require precise weight-based dosing

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of intense itching on the palms, sides of the fingers, or soles, followed rapidly by deep, semi-transparent small vesicles resembling 'sago'. The vesicles are usually grouped; after several weeks they dry and desquamate, exposing red, tender skin with pain or burning. Symptoms often worsen in spring and summer and tend to recur, often related to psychological stress or contact with irritants.

first_questions: Have you developed clustered small blisters on your hands and feet with intense itching?
Are these symptoms seasonal or persistent? Have you recently contacted detergents or metals?
followup_questions: If the blisters rupture, is there any exudation or sign of secondary infection (such as redness, swelling, heat, and pain)?
Have you recently been under high stress or do you have a history of eczema or allergy?
stop_conditions: The typical blister morphology, location, and itching characteristics have been clearly described.
Common triggers and manifestations of fungal infection (such as tinea manuum) have been excluded.
It has been confirmed that there is no systemic rash or other systemic disease symptoms.

essential: Dermoscopy (to observe deep vesicles and epidermal structure)
Fungal microscopy (KOH smear, to exclude tinea manuum/pedis)
if_suspected: Patch test (to screen for contact allergens)
Serum IgE testing (to assess atopic constitution)
avoid: Unnecessary routine tests before systemic corticosteroid therapy
Extensive blood cultures for simple localized lesions

first_line: First-line treatment is topical potent corticosteroids (e.g., halometasone cream), twice daily for 1-2 weeks until the vesicles resolve

In the acute phase, cold wet compresses can be used for astringent effect. If itching is severe, oral antihistamines (e.g., loratadine) may be used. Nonpharmacologic interventions include avoiding contact with irritating chemicals, keeping the hands dry, and stress reduction.
safety_warnings: Long-term large-area use of potent corticosteroids may cause skin atrophy or telangiectasia; the course must be strictly controlled according to medical advice.
Use corticosteroids with caution when there is concurrent bacterial infection; the infection should be controlled first.
Avoid applying corticosteroid ointments to the face or severely broken skin to prevent excessive absorption.
personalization: Pediatric patients should use medium- to low-potency corticosteroids and a shortened course.
Pregnant women require physician assessment and weighing of risks and benefits, with priority given to physical therapy or low-potency preparations.
Patients with occupational exposure need reinforced use of protective gloves to reduce recurrence.

skills.presentation: Patients often present with sudden-onset, densely distributed, painful, umbilicated vesicles or pustules on a background of pre-existing atopic dermatitis or eczema. The lesions show centrifugal spread, accompanied by marked erythema, swelling, erosion, and crusting. Systemic symptoms are prominent, including high fever, chills, fatigue, and regional lymphadenopathy. The rash morphology closely resembles varicella but is more severe, is prone to secondary bacterial infection, and carries a risk of sepsis.

first_questions: Has the eczema or dermatitis on your body suddenly worsened recently?
Have you had fever, chills, or extreme fatigue?
Is there obvious pain in the rash areas rather than just itching?
followup_questions: Have you recently been in contact with anyone who has herpes simplex or varicella?
Where did the rash start spreading from, and how fast has it progressed?
Have any skin ointments or corticosteroid medications you previously used been adjusted recently?
stop_conditions: Primary skin disease history is clear and typical umbilicated vesicles with high fever are present.
The patient has received antiviral treatment and vital signs are stabilizing.
Necessary virologic testing has been completed and other infectious diseases have been excluded.

essential: Tzanck smear (looking for multinucleated giant cells)
HSV-1/2 PCR nucleic acid testing
Complete blood count and C-reactive protein testing
if_suspected: Bacterial culture (to evaluate secondary Staphylococcus aureus infection)
Serologic antibody testing (IgM/IgG)
Liver and kidney function assessment (to assess risk of severe disease)
avoid: Routine skin biopsy (unless the diagnosis is unclear and noninvasive tests are negative)
Unnecessary combined use of broad-spectrum antibiotics (before bacterial infection is confirmed)
Topical potent glucocorticoids (may worsen viral infection)

first_line: Immediately initiate systemic antiviral therapy, with intravenous acyclovir as first choice (10mg/kg every 8 hours) for 7-14 days, until new lesions stop appearing. If the disease is mild, oral valacyclovir can be used instead. At the same time, provide symptomatic supportive treatment, such as antipyretics, fluid replacement, and analgesia. Strictly prohibit the use of glucocorticoid ointment on the original lesion to prevent viral spread.
safety_warnings: Patients with renal impairment require acyclovir dose adjustment based on creatinine clearance to prevent nephrotoxicity.
Avoid concomitant use with nephrotoxic drugs (such as aminoglycosides).
Be alert for central nervous system adverse reactions, such as confusion or tremor.
personalization: Infants and older adults require close monitoring of dehydration and electrolyte balance.
Immunosuppressed patients (such as after organ transplantation) require prolonged treatment and enhanced monitoring.
Drug use in pregnant women requires weighing benefits and risks, with consultation of an obstetric specialist when necessary.

skills.presentation: Patients often report a slowly enlarging painless subcutaneous mass, of medium to firm consistency, with a smooth surface. A typical feature is a pinpoint-sized black dot in the center (the cyst opening); when squeezed, white cheesy foul-smelling contents can be expressed. If secondary infection occurs, it presents as local erythema, swelling, heat, and pain, and may even form an abscess that ruptures and drains pus.

first_questions: How long has this lump been present? Has its growth rate increased recently?
Is it painful when pressed? Has it previously become red, swollen, or ruptured and drained pus?
followup_questions: If it has ruptured before, was the discharge white and cheesy with an odor?
Has this area been injured or subjected to long-term friction/irritation?
stop_conditions: The morphology, size, and history of infection of the mass have been clearly described.
It is confirmed that there are no malignant signs such as recent rapid enlargement, fixation, or systemic symptoms.
The patient indicates that no further history taking is needed before physical examination.

essential: Inspection and palpation: observe the mass morphology, color, central opening, and fluctuation.
Ultrasound: assess the cyst boundary, internal echogenicity, and relationship with surrounding tissues.
if_suspected: Pathologic biopsy: perform when keratoacanthoma or squamous cell carcinoma is suspected.
Bacterial culture: obtain a sample when secondary infection is severe and antibiotic treatment is ineffective.
avoid: Blind puncture and aspiration: easily leads to cyst wall rupture and spread of inflammation.
Routine X-ray: has very low diagnostic value for soft-tissue cysts.

first_line: For asymptomatic patients, complete surgical excision of the cyst wall is the first choice to prevent recurrence. The incision should be designed along skin tension lines to avoid damaging the cyst wall. If secondary infection has already occurred, first perform incision and drainage and give oral antibiotics (such as cephalosporins) to control inflammation; after inflammation subsides, perform elective excision in 3-6 months. Nonpharmacologic interventions include avoiding squeezing and friction at the affected site.
safety_warnings: Strictly prohibit forced squeezing before infection control, to prevent infection spreading to deep tissues.
During excision, the cyst wall must be completely removed; residual cyst wall is the main cause of recurrence.
Pay attention to wound care after surgery to prevent secondary bacterial infection.
personalization: Patients with diabetes need strengthened glycemic control and prolonged antibiotic courses to prevent persistent infection.
Patients with a tendency to scar formation need adequate preoperative communication; cosmetic suture techniques are recommended to reduce scarring.
Facial cysts require meticulous operation to protect hair follicles and neurovascular structures and reduce cosmetic impact.

skills.presentation: Patients often report sudden onset of symmetrically distributed red macules and papules that rapidly evolve into target or iris lesions, commonly on the dorsal hands and feet, forearms, and extensor aspects of the lower legs. Some patients have mucosal involvement, such as congestion, erosion, and pain of the oral, ocular, or genital mucosa, and may have systemic symptoms such as fever and fatigue. The typical manifestation is a 'target lesion,' a three-layer structure with a dark red center, a surrounding edema ring, and an outermost pale red halo.

first_questions: Within 1-3 weeks before the rash appeared, did you have a cold, fever, or start taking a new medication?
Is the rash mainly distributed on the hands and feet, face, or extensor aspects of the limbs?
Do you have pain, ulcers, or increased secretions in your mouth or eyes?
followup_questions: If you mentioned taking medication, which specific drug was it (such as sulfonamides or antibiotics)?
If you mentioned infection, have you had a recent recurrence of herpes simplex?
Are the mucosal lesions affecting your ability to eat or your vision?
stop_conditions: Typical target lesion distribution and mucosal involvement have been clearly identified.
Recent triggers (drugs or infection) have been confirmed.
