first_line: First-line treatment is a potent topical corticosteroid (e.g., halometasone cream), twice daily for 4 consecutive weeks, combined with occlusion therapy to enhance penetration. For refractory nodules, local injection of triamcinolone acetonide suspension may be used. At the same time, oral antihistamines (e.g., cetirizine 10 mg/day) control itching. Non-pharmacologic interventions include strict avoidance of scratching, use of emollients to repair the barrier, and cold compresses to relieve itching.
safety_warnings: Long-term large-area use of potent corticosteroids may cause skin atrophy and telangiectasia and requires regular monitoring.
Local block injection requires strict aseptic technique to prevent infection and the risk of subcutaneous fat atrophy.
Oral antihistamines may cause drowsiness; caution is needed when driving or operating machinery.
personalization: Pediatric patients should use medium- to low-potency corticosteroids, and the course should be shortened to avoid affecting growth and development.
Pregnant and breastfeeding women must not use retinoids; corticosteroid use requires weighing benefits and risks under physician guidance.
Older patients have thin, fragile skin; corticosteroid concentration should be reduced and moisturization strengthened to prevent fissures and infection.

skills.presentation: Patients complain of intense itching of the skin around the anus, often worsened at night and affecting sleep. Itching is paroxysmal or continuous and may lead to skin thickening, lichenification, erosion, or secondary infection due to scratching. Some patients have a feeling of dampness or burning pain; symptoms recur and remain unrelieved after routine cleaning.

first_questions: How long has the itching lasted? Is it worse during the day or at night?
Have you recently had diarrhea, constipation, or fecal incontinence?
Have you used any ointments or lotions on your own, and how effective were they?
followup_questions: If there is a change in stool characteristics, ask: 'Have you recently eaten spicy or irritating foods or consumed alcohol?'
If a rash is found, ask: 'Is there exudation, bleeding, or visible worms at the itchy area?'
If allergy is suspected, ask: 'Have you changed toilet paper, underwear material, or used wet wipes?'
stop_conditions: Parasitic infection (such as pinworm) and history of sexually transmitted diseases have been clearly excluded.
It has been confirmed that there is no systemic underlying disease such as diabetes or hepatobiliary disease.
The symptoms described by the patient are typical and there are no warning symptoms (such as hematochezia or mass).

essential: Anal visual inspection and digital examination
Stool routine and occult blood test
Microscopic examination of perianal skin scrapings (to rule out fungal/parasitic infection)
if_suspected: Blood glucose measurement (to rule out diabetes)
Colonoscopy (if intestinal lesions are suspected)
Patch test (to rule out contact dermatitis)
avoid: Unnecessary long-term use of broad-spectrum antibiotics
Long-term topical use of high-concentration corticosteroid ointments
Invasive biopsy (unless tumor is suspected)

first_line: First-line treatment includes local care and pharmacologic intervention. Keep the perianal area dry and clean; avoid washing with hot water. Apply a low- to medium-potency topical corticosteroid ointment (e.g., hydrocortisone cream) twice daily for no more than 2 weeks.

When complicated by fungal infection, combine with an antifungal agent (e.g., clotrimazole). Oral antihistamines (e.g., loratadine 10 mg qd) relieve nighttime itching. Non-pharmacologic interventions include wearing cotton underwear, avoiding spicy foods, and breaking the scratching habit.
safety_warnings: Long-term large-area use of potent corticosteroids is strictly prohibited to prevent skin atrophy and telangiectasia.
Be careful to distinguish eczema from tinea cruris; misuse of corticosteroids may worsen fungal infection.
If signs of secondary bacterial infection appear, promptly discontinue corticosteroids and add antibiotics.
personalization: For pediatric patients, low-potency corticosteroids are preferred, with strict control of treatment duration to prevent growth suppression.
Older adults have thin, fragile skin; medication frequency should be reduced and moisturizing repair strengthened.
Pregnant women should use oral antihistamines with caution; physical cooling and local cold compresses are preferred.

skills.presentation: Patients complain of painless areas of hair loss on the scalp, often accompanied by local skin atrophy, shininess, and loss of follicular ostia. At the edges of the hair loss areas, residual hairs may be arranged in a 'tufted' or 'comb-tooth-like' pattern, without inflammatory redness, swelling, or scaling. The course is slow, mostly on the vertex or temporal region, easily misdiagnosed as ordinary alopecia areata, but lacks a tendency for spontaneous remission and involves irreversible destruction of hair follicles.

first_questions: Is the hair loss area accompanied by itching, pain, or burning?
Is there redness, crusting, or scaling on the skin surface of the hair loss area?
followup_questions: Does the skin in the hair loss area feel smoother or depressed compared with the surrounding skin?
Has this area previously had trauma, infection, or long-term pressure?
stop_conditions: The patient clearly describes skin atrophy, shininess, and no inflammatory reaction in the hair loss area.
It has been confirmed that the follicular ostia in the hair loss area have disappeared and there are no signs of new hair growth.
Typical symptoms of active inflammatory skin diseases (such as discoid lupus erythematosus) have been excluded.

essential: Dermoscopy (observe loss of follicular ostia and scarring features)
Skin biopsy with pathologic examination (gold standard for diagnosis)
if_suspected: Direct immunofluorescence examination (to rule out autoimmune blistering diseases)
Fungal microscopy and culture (to rule out tinea capitis)
avoid: Routine complete blood count (nonspecific and not directly helpful for diagnosis)
Trace element testing (unrelated to the cause of scarring alopecia)

first_line: There is currently no specific curative method; the focus of treatment is to control inflammation to prevent extension. The first-line regimen is local injection of corticosteroids (e.g., triamcinolone acetonide), once every 4 weeks for 3–6 consecutive months.

in combination with a potent topical corticosteroid ointment. For early active disease, oral hydroxychloroquine may be added. Non-pharmacologic interventions include avoiding local friction and pressure, and hair transplantation for repair when necessary (after the disease is stable).
safety_warnings: Local injection requires vigilance for the risk of subcutaneous fat atrophy and skin hypopigmentation.
Long-term use of potent corticosteroids may cause skin thinning or telangiectasia.
Oral hydroxychloroquine requires regular fundus monitoring to prevent retinal toxicity.
personalization: Pediatric patients should use systemic drugs with caution; low-concentration topical corticosteroids are preferred.
Pregnant women must not use teratogenic drugs such as methotrexate; the treatment plan needs to be adjusted.
Older patients should be monitored for changes in skin absorption, and corticosteroid dosage should be appropriately reduced.

skills.presentation: Patients often report a rapidly growing red or purplish-red nodule on the skin or mucosa, with a smooth or lobulated surface, which bleeds easily. The lesion is usually painless, but may cause pain or discomfort when touched. It commonly occurs on exposed areas such as the face and fingers, and some patients have a history of trauma.

first_questions: How long ago did you notice this mass? Has it rapidly enlarged over a short period?
Have you had any trauma or surgery in this area?
Does the mass bleed easily? How often does it bleed?
followup_questions: If the mass is on the face or another visible area, does it affect your daily life or appearance?
Do you have any other associated symptoms, such as fever or local redness, swelling, heat, or pain?
Do you have a history of similar lesions or a family history?
stop_conditions: The growth rate of the mass, bleeding status, and history of trauma have been clarified.
The patient has no other systemic symptoms (such as fever or general malaise).
The presentation is initially assessed as typical, and further questioning is not needed.

essential: Dermoscopy: observe vascular morphology and distribution characteristics.
Histopathological examination: confirm whether it is pyogenic granuloma.
if_suspected: Ultrasound: assess lesion depth and involvement of surrounding tissues.
Immunohistochemical staining: rule out other vascular or neoplastic diseases.
avoid: Unnecessary whole-body imaging (such as CT or MRI), unless deep invasion is suspected.
Repeat biopsy, to avoid excessive trauma.

first_line: First-line treatment includes local excision combined with electrocoagulation for hemostasis, which is suitable for most cases. For smaller lesions, laser therapy (such as pulsed dye laser) may be considered. For pharmacotherapy, beta-blockers (such as timolol) can be used to inhibit vascular proliferation. The course of treatment is usually 1-2 weeks, with regular follow-up to monitor for recurrence. Nonpharmacologic interventions include avoiding friction and irritation of the affected area.
safety_warnings: Contraindications: use excision with caution in patients allergic to local anesthetics.
Drug interactions: monitor heart rate and blood pressure when using beta-blockers.
Prevention of serious adverse reactions: the risk of postoperative infection should be reduced through aseptic technique.
personalization: For pediatric patients, minimally invasive treatment is preferred to reduce scar formation.
Pregnant women should avoid systemic drugs and receive only local physical therapy.
Immunocompromised patients require strengthened postoperative infection management.

skills.presentation: Patients often develop erythema and edema on exposed skin hours to 1-2 days after sun exposure, accompanied by a burning sensation or stinging. In severe cases, vesicles, bullae, and erosions with exudation may occur. The lesions have clear borders, correspond to the light-exposed areas, and the non-exposed areas are normal. Itching is common, and some patients have systemic symptoms such as fever and fatigue.

first_questions: Did the rash appear after intense sun exposure? What was the specific interval?
Which body areas are mainly affected by the rash (such as the face and arms)?
Have you recently used any medications or cosmetics that may increase photosensitivity?
followup_questions: If blisters are present, is there severe pain or exudation?
Do you have a history of similar episodes or a family history of allergy?
Do the symptoms improve after avoiding light?
stop_conditions: The history of sun exposure is clear and the lesion morphology is typical; no further questioning about triggers is needed.
No history of systemic medication use or special occupational exposure has been confirmed.
The patient reports mild symptoms and no systemic reaction.

essential: Dermoscopy
Wood's lamp examination
Patch test (to rule out contact factors)
if_suspected: Ultraviolet irradiation test (to determine the sensitizing wavelength)
Serum IgE testing (to screen for atopic constitution)
Photoprovocation test
avoid: Routine bacterial culture (unless there is clear evidence of secondary infection)
Unnecessary whole-body CT scanning

first_line: First-line treatment includes immediately removing the patient from sun exposure and applying local cold wet compresses to reduce redness and swelling. Topical corticosteroid ointment (such as 0.1% mometasone furoate), twice daily for 5-7 days. Oral antihistamines (such as loratadine 10 mg once daily) to relieve itching. For severe cases, short-term oral prednisone 30-40 mg/day, with gradual tapering. Physical sun protection and repair of the skin barrier are also recommended.
safety_warnings: Avoid long-term, large-area use of potent corticosteroids to prevent skin atrophy
Be aware of the risk of combining corticosteroids with immunosuppressants
Watch for secondary bacterial infection and add antibiotics if necessary
personalization: Children should use low-potency corticosteroids and a shorter course
Pregnant women should use systemic drugs with caution, with local treatment preferred
Older adults should be aware of the risk of skin thinning and avoid potent formulations

skills.presentation: Within minutes to half an hour after exposure to sunlight (especially UVA/UVB), patients develop pruritic wheals, erythema, or edema on the skin. The typical presentation is a rash that appears rapidly on sun-exposed areas and resolves within 1-24 hours after avoiding light, without leaving marks. A burning sensation or stinging is common, and severe cases may have systemic reactions such as dizziness, palpitations, or even anaphylactic shock. The symptoms show a clear seasonal pattern and relationship to light exposure.

first_questions: Did the rash appear within minutes after sun exposure?
How long does it take for the rash to resolve completely after avoiding sunlight?
Do you have systemic symptoms such as difficulty breathing or dizziness?
followup_questions: If a specific wavelength is suspected as the trigger, ask: does it also occur on cloudy days or with sunlight through a glass window?
If symptoms recur, ask: have you recently taken photosensitizing drugs (such as tetracyclines or diuretics)?
If the condition is severe, ask: do you have a history of similar allergy or a family history?
stop_conditions: The temporal relationship between sun exposure and onset has been clarified, and there is no systemic crisis.
It has been confirmed that no photosensitizing drugs have been used recently.
The patient reports typical symptoms and avoidance measures are effective.

essential: Sunlight provocation test (to determine the minimal urticarial dose)
Dermatographism test (to rule out other physical urticarias)
if_suspected: Photopatch test (to differentiate photoallergic contact dermatitis)
Serum IgE and eosinophil count (to assess atopic constitution)
avoid: Routine bacterial culture (noninfectious disease)
Unnecessary CT/MRI examinations (no evidence of structural lesions)

first_line: First-line treatment is a second-generation nonsedating antihistamine (such as cetirizine 10 mg qd or loratadine 10 mg qd), with dose doubling if necessary. During acute attacks, short-term oral corticosteroids (such as prednisone 30 mg/day for 3-5 days) may be used. The core nonpharmacologic intervention is strict sun protection, including wearing long-sleeved clothing, using broad-spectrum sunscreen (SPF50+, PA++++), and avoiding going out at midday.
safety_warnings: Avoid long-term use of first-generation antihistamines to prevent central nervous system depression and fall risk
Corticosteroids must not be stopped abruptly; taper gradually to prevent rebound
Watch for rare phototoxic drug interactions; review prescriptions before use
personalization: In children, adjust antihistamine doses by body weight and prefer formulations with a high safety profile
Pregnant women should use corticosteroids with caution; physical sun protection and topical calcineurin inhibitors are preferred
In older adults, be aware of the effects of antihistamines on cognitive function and advise avoiding driving or operating machinery

skills.presentation: Patients often report a painless genital ulcer (chancre), accompanied by inguinal lymphadenopathy. Secondary syphilis presents with symmetric generalized erythema and papules, especially copper-red macules on the palms and soles, and may be accompanied by systemic symptoms such as fever, fatigue, and hair loss. Late syphilis may involve the cardiovascular or nervous system, manifesting as blurred vision, headache, gait instability, and other symptoms.

first_questions: Do you have a history of unsafe sexual practices?
Have you recently noticed a genital ulcer or rash?
Do you have any systemic discomfort such as fever or fatigue?
followup_questions: If you have noticed an ulcer, please describe its size, whether it is painful, and how long it has lasted.
Is the rash accompanied by itching or scaling?
Do you have any history of similar symptoms or previous treatment?
stop_conditions: A history of unsafe sexual practices has been clarified, and typical symptoms are present.
Laboratory testing has confirmed the infection.
The patient declines to provide further information, and the symptoms are typical.

essential: Nontreponemal antibody testing (RPR/TRUST)
Treponemal antibody testing (TPPA/TPHA)
Darkfield microscopy (of ulcer exudate)
if_suspected: Cerebrospinal fluid examination (when neurosyphilis is suspected)
Cardiovascular imaging (when cardiovascular syphilis is suspected)
Screening for HIV and other sexually transmitted infections
avoid: Routine X-ray examination (when there is no clear indication)
Unnecessary tissue biopsy (when serologic evidence is already present)
Repeating the same type of serologic testing

first_line: First-line treatment is benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units as a single intramuscular injection. Early syphilis requires completion of one course.

Late syphilis requires once weekly for 3 consecutive weeks. For patients allergic to penicillin, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14-28 days may be selected. Patients and their sexual partners should also be advised to undergo screening and treatment.
safety_warnings: Contraindicated in patients allergic to penicillin; allergy history should be assessed in advance.
Avoid concomitant use with anticoagulants such as warfarin to prevent an increased bleeding risk.
Watch for the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, especially in pregnant patients or those with neurosyphilis.
personalization: Pregnant patients must receive penicillin; no substitute is acceptable.
Pediatric doses should be adjusted according to body weight.
In patients with hepatic or renal impairment, drug metabolism should be monitored.

skills.presentation: Patients often report annular or polycyclic erythematous lesions on the trunk or limbs, with raised scaling borders and central clearing that gradually produces an imbricate appearance. Lesions may be mildly pruritic, worse in summer and less severe in winter. Typical findings are multiple concentric scaly plaques with well-defined borders, requiring differentiation from tinea corporis and psoriasis.

first_questions: How long have the rash lesions been present? Have they gradually enlarged or increased in number?
Is there significant itching? Does it worsen after sweating?
Have you recently had contact with pets or a history of similar skin disease?
followup_questions: If your rash has spread in a ring, have you ever used corticosteroid ointments on your own?
If the itching is severe, does it affect your sleep or daily activities?
If it recurs, is there a family history of similar cases?
stop_conditions: The patient clearly describes typical annular lesions and has no systemic symptoms.
Sufficient history has been provided and the patient has cooperated with skin examination.
Manifestations related to other systemic diseases (such as autoimmune disease) have been excluded.

essential: Fungal microscopy of skin scrapings
Wood's lamp examination
Skin biopsy of the lesion site (if necessary)
if_suspected: Serologic testing (to exclude systemic fungal infection)
Allergen testing (to differentiate contact dermatitis)
Skin confocal microscopy (adjunctive diagnosis)
avoid: Routine complete blood count (nonspecific)
Unnecessary imaging studies (such as CT/MRI)
Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy (when there is no evidence of bacterial infection)

first_line: First-line treatment is topical antifungal agents, such as bifonazole cream once daily for 2-4 weeks

For severe or extensive disease, oral itraconazole 200 mg/day for 7-14 days. At the same time, keep the affected area dry and clean and avoid scratching. Nonpharmacologic interventions include wearing breathable clothing and regularly disinfecting personal items.
safety_warnings: Use oral antifungals with caution in patients with abnormal liver function, and monitor liver enzymes.
Avoid coadministration with CYP3A4 inhibitors (such as ketoconazole) to prevent increased toxicity.
Oral drugs are contraindicated in pregnant and breastfeeding women; topical use should follow medical advice.
personalization: For pediatric patients, reduce the dose of oral drugs and prefer topical formulations.
In older adults, note that drug metabolism is slowed and extend the observation period.
For immunosuppressed patients, jointly assess infection risk and adjust the regimen.

skills.presentation: Patients often report hand itching, especially worsening at night or after contact with water. The skin shows erythema, scaling, vesicles, or hyperkeratosis, commonly on the palms, finger webs, and around the nails. Some patients have fissures and pain, or even secondary bacterial infection causing redness, swelling, warmth, and pain. Symptoms are often unilateral or asymmetrical and are easily confused with eczema.

first_questions: How long has your hand itching lasted? Is it symmetrical?
Do you have a history of athlete's foot or fungal infection at other sites?
followup_questions: Do your symptoms worsen in damp environments or after sweating?
Have you tried medication? How effective was it?
stop_conditions: Unilateral onset is confirmed and is accompanied by typical scaling or vesicles.
There is a history of tinea pedis and symptoms are consistent with fungal infection.
Common differential diagnoses such as eczema have been excluded.

essential: Fungal microscopy (KOH preparation)
Fungal culture
if_suspected: Skin biopsy (for atypical cases)
Wood's lamp examination
avoid: Systemic imaging studies without indication
Nonspecific allergen testing

first_line: First-line treatment is topical antifungal agents, such as bifonazole cream or terbinafine cream, once or twice daily for at least 4 weeks. For the hyperkeratotic type, urea ointment may be used in combination to soften keratin. Keep the hands dry and avoid contact with irritants.
safety_warnings: Avoid long-term use of corticosteroid ointments over large areas.
Contraindicated in patients allergic to azoles or allylamines.
Note that drugs may cause local irritation reactions.
personalization: For children, reduce dosing frequency and monitor for adverse reactions.
For pregnant women, prefer topical medication and consult a physician.
For patients with diabetes, strengthen care to prevent secondary infection.

skills.presentation: Patients often report severe itching, stinging, or a foreign-body sensation in the feet or between the toes, with paroxysmal exacerbations. On examination, tiny red papules, vesicles, or scratch marks may be seen in the toe webs or on the soles, and in some cases tiny black or brown dots under the skin (adult fleas) are visible; surrounding skin may show redness and swelling or secondary infection due to scratching. Symptoms often worsen after walking barefoot on grass or carpet or after contact with pets.

first_questions: Have you recently been to grass, parks, or had contact with pets such as cats and dogs?
Do you have a noticeable stinging sensation at the affected area or feel something moving under the skin?
followup_questions: If there is redness, swelling, or oozing, please describe the severity and duration of the pain.
Has anyone else in your household developed similar symptoms?
stop_conditions: Recent exposure to grass has been confirmed and symptoms are typical.
Physical examination has revealed a subdermal organism or characteristic skin lesions.
The patient has received initial management and there are no signs of serious complications.

essential: Dermoscopy (to observe subdermal organisms and burrows)
Transparent tape preparation (to collect organisms or eggs)
Microscopic examination of scrapings from the lesion
if_suspected: Bacterial culture (to exclude secondary bacterial infection)
Fungal microscopy (to differentiate tinea pedis)
avoid: Unnecessary whole-body CT or MRI
Routine complete blood count (unless serious systemic infection is suspected)

first_line: First-line treatment is local physical removal: use a sterile needle to puncture the epidermis and remove the organism, then disinfect with povidone-iodine. Apply a topical antibiotic ointment (such as mupirocin ointment) twice daily for 5-7 days to prevent infection. If itching is severe, a short course of oral antihistamines (such as loratadine 10 mg once daily) may be used. At the same time, thoroughly clean the environment, wash clothing, and dry it at high temperature to prevent reinfection.
safety_warnings: Do not squeeze the organism, to prevent toxin spread or allergic reactions.
Povidone-iodine disinfection is contraindicated in patients allergic to iodine preparations.
Avoid long-term use of potent corticosteroids over large areas to prevent masking infection.
personalization: For children, adjust drug doses by body weight and avoid strongly irritating disinfectants.
Use oral drugs with caution in pregnant women; prefer physical removal and gentle local treatment.
For patients with diabetes, strengthen wound care and closely monitor for signs of infection.

skills.presentation: Patients often report painless, flat, yellow plaques on the inner aspect of the eyelids or near the inner canthus, with a soft texture and well-defined borders. Lesions are often symmetrical; initially they may appear only as slight elevations and gradually enlarge and coalesce over time. They are usually asymptomatic and do not affect vision, but patients often seek care because of cosmetic concerns. Some patients may have a history of dyslipidemia.

first_questions: How long ago did you notice the yellow plaques on your eyelids? Have they recently become larger or increased in number?
Apart from the cosmetic change, do you have any eye discomfort such as redness, swelling, pain, or blurred vision?
Do you or your first-degree relatives have a history of hyperlipidemia, coronary heart disease, or diabetes?
followup_questions: If the plaques have recently enlarged rapidly or ulcerated, is there any discharge or bleeding?
Is your usual diet high in fat? Do you have long-term smoking or alcohol use?
Have you previously received lipid-lowering treatment? Are you currently taking statins?
stop_conditions: The morphologic features of the lesions (yellow, flat, located at the inner canthus) have been confirmed and there are no signs of acute inflammation.
Key family history and information on underlying diseases (such as hyperlipidemia) have been obtained.
The patient has a preliminary understanding of the treatment plan, and further questioning about nonspecific symptoms is not needed.

essential: Complete physical examination (focusing on whether similar lesions are present on other skin areas)
Fasting lipid panel (total cholesterol, triglycerides, LDL-C, HDL-C)
if_suspected: Liver and kidney function tests (to assess metabolic status and medication safety)
Carotid ultrasound (to screen for atherosclerotic plaques)
Fundus examination (to exclude retinal vascular disease)
avoid: Routine skin biopsy (typical cases do not require pathologic confirmation; avoid scarring)
Unnecessary systemic tumor screening (unless other suspicious signs are present)
Repeated lipid testing (if there is no need to adjust treatment)

first_line: First-line treatment targets the underlying cause, namely strict control of lipid levels through dietary intervention (low-fat, low-sugar) and oral lipid-lowering drugs (such as statins) to improve metabolism. For patients with strong cosmetic concerns, local treatment may be considered: laser ablation (CO2 laser) or chemical peeling (trichloroacetic acid), which must be performed by a professional physician to control depth and avoid scar formation. Physical excision is suitable for larger lesions but has a higher recurrence rate.
safety_warnings: Do not self-apply corrosive drugs topically, to avoid eyelid skin necrosis or severe scarring.
When using trichloroacetic acid, strictly protect the conjunctiva and cornea to prevent chemical burns.
If severe cardiovascular disease is present, assess anesthesia and stress risks before surgery or laser treatment.
personalization: For older patients, assess skin elasticity and carefully select energy parameters to prevent poor healing.
Systemic lipid-lowering drugs and invasive treatment are contraindicated in pregnant and breastfeeding women; postpartum management is recommended.
For patients with diabetes, strengthen postprocedural blood glucose monitoring to prevent infection and delayed healing.

skills.presentation: Patients often report pruritus and a tight sensation, which worsen especially in autumn and winter or after bathing. Scaling and roughness may be visible on the skin surface, and in severe cases fissures or erythema may occur. Symptoms are mostly distributed on the extensor aspects of the limbs, back, and abdomen, and scratching may lead to secondary skin lesions.

first_questions: Does your skin often feel itchy or tight?
Under what circumstances do these symptoms worsen (e.g., after bathing or when seasons change)?
followup_questions: Do you use irritating bathing products or have a habit of bathing frequently?
Is there a family history of eczema or other allergic diseases?
stop_conditions: The patient clearly describes typical symptoms and has no manifestations of other systemic diseases
Triggers have been confirmed (e.g., dry environment, overcleaning) and other skin diseases have been excluded
The patient understands the treatment recommendations and is willing to cooperate

essential: Skin inspection and palpation
Skin hydration measurement (Corneometer)
if_suspected: Allergen testing (if atopic dermatitis is suspected)
Thyroid function tests (to exclude endocrine factors)
avoid: Unnecessary skin biopsy (unless another disease is suspected)
Routine blood cultures (when there is no evidence of infection)

first_line: First-line treatment includes daily use of moisturizers containing urea, ceramides, or glycerol, once in the morning and once in the evening. Avoid washing with hot water; switch to a mild, soap-free cleanser. If pruritus is severe, a low-potency topical corticosteroid ointment (e.g., hydrocortisone cream) may be used short-term for no more than 2 weeks. It is also recommended to increase indoor humidity to 40%–60%.
safety_warnings: Avoid long-term use of potent corticosteroids to prevent skin atrophy or pigmentation
Pay attention to moisturizer ingredients; avoid products containing alcohol or fragrance that may cause irritation
If signs of secondary infection occur (e.g., pustules, worsening redness and swelling), seek medical attention promptly
personalization: Older adults should choose more emollient formulations to reduce penetration-related irritation
For pediatric patients, prioritize fragrance-free, hypoallergenic formulations
Patients with diabetes should strengthen foot care to prevent infection of fissures
